content: During pregnancy, fetal cells for genetic testing can be obtained through amniocentesis (AC), which involves sampling amniotic fluid, or chorionic villus sampling (CVS), which involves sampling placental tissue. A significant limitation of second-trimester amniocentesis is that results are only available after 16 weeks of gestation, which is relatively late in pregnancy. Earlier alternatives include CVS and early amniocentesis, both of which can be performed during the first trimester. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the safety and accuracy of various types of amniocentesis (early and late) and CVS (transabdominal and transcervical) for prenatal diagnosis. The review included 16 randomized studies involving 33,555 women, with 14 studies considered to have a low risk of bias. The studies were grouped into six comparisons: second-trimester AC versus no testing, early versus second-trimester AC, CVS versus second-trimester AC, different CVS methods, early AC versus CVS, and AC with or without ultrasound guidance. One study involving 4,606 women compared second-trimester AC with no testing in a low-risk population. The baseline pregnancy loss rate was approximately 2%. Second-trimester AC increased the total pregnancy loss rate by an additional 1% (3.2% versus 2.3%; risk ratio [RR] 1.41, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.99 to 2.00; moderate-quality evidence). Spontaneous miscarriage rates were also higher in the AC group (2.1% versus 1.3%; RR 1.60, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.52; high-quality evidence). The incidence of congenital anomalies was similar between the two groups (2.0% versus 2.2%; RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.39; moderate-quality evidence). Another study involving 4,334 women found that early amniocentesis was not as safe as second-trimester amniocentesis. Early AC was associated with higher rates of total pregnancy loss (7.6% versus 5.9%; RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.61; high-quality evidence), spontaneous miscarriages (3.6% versus 2.5%; RR 1.41, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.98; moderate-quality evidence), and congenital anomalies, including talipes (4.7% versus 2.7%; RR 1.73, 95% CI 1.26 to 2.38; high-quality evidence). When comparing pregnancy loss after CVS with second-trimester AC, the results varied significantly depending on the technique used (transabdominal or transcervical), so the data could not be pooled. One study involving 2,234 women compared transabdominal CVS with second-trimester AC and found no significant differences in total pregnancy loss (6.3% versus 7%; RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.23; low-quality evidence), spontaneous miscarriages (3.0% versus 3.9%; RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.21; low-quality evidence), or perinatal deaths (0.7% versus 0.6%; RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.40 to 3.51; low-quality evidence). Transcervical CVS may carry a higher risk of pregnancy loss compared to transabdominal CVS (14.5% versus 11.5%; RR 1.40, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.81), but the results were highly variable. Five studies involving 7,978 women compared transabdominal and transcervical CVS. No significant differences were found in pregnancy loss rates (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.65; very low-quality evidence), spontaneous miscarriage rates (RR 1.68, 95% CI 0.79 to 3.58; very low-quality evidence), or congenital anomalies (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.12; low-quality evidence). However, transcervical CVS was more technically challenging, with a higher rate of failed sample collection (2.0% versus 1.1%; RR 1.79, 95% CI 1.13 to 2.82; moderate-quality evidence). When early amniocentesis was compared to transabdominal CVS, the evidence was of low quality overall. Spontaneous miscarriage was the only outcome supported by moderate-quality evidence, with more miscarriages occurring after early AC compared to transabdominal CVS (2.3% versus 1.3%; RR 1.73, 95% CI 1.15 to 2.60). There were no significant differences in total pregnancy loss (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.54; low-quality evidence) or congenital anomalies (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.57 to 2.30; very low-quality evidence). One study examined amniocentesis with and without ultrasound guidance, but the ultrasound-assisted procedure evaluated is now considered outdated. In conclusion, second-trimester amniocentesis increases the risk of pregnancy loss, but the exact magnitude of this risk is uncertain due to limited data from a single study conducted over 30 years ago. Early amniocentesis is less safe than second-trimester amniocentesis, with higher rates of pregnancy loss and congenital anomalies such as talipes. Transcervical CVS may be associated with a higher risk of pregnancy loss compared to second-trimester amniocentesis, but the results are inconsistent. The diagnostic accuracy of these methods could not be adequately assessed due to incomplete karyotype data in most studies.
